title: 2 Samuel 20:1–3
context: The quarrel of 19:40–43 gives an opening to Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite whom the narrator calls a wicked fellow, who blows the trumpet and calls Israel away from David. The men of Israel follow Sheba, while Judah stays with the king from the Jordan to Jerusalem. On returning home, David places the ten concubines he had left to keep the house (2 Samuel 15:16), and whom Absalom had publicly violated (2 Samuel 16:22), in custody, provides for them, and has no further relations with them, so that they live in widowhood until they die. An ancient scribal tradition reports that the phrase to his tents in verse 1 was altered from a word meaning to his gods, though the received text reads tents. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about the spread of division and the lasting human cost of sin within a household.

verses.text: There happened to be there a wicked fellow, whose name was Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite; and he blew the trumpet, and said, “We have no portion in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse. Every man to his tents, Israel!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sheba, called a wicked fellow, blowing the trumpet and calling Israel away from David. Division is exploited by a troublemaker.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his cry echoed later when the kingdom divides (1 Kings 12:16). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how quickly unity can collapse.

verses.text: So all the men of Israel went up from following David, and followed Sheba the son of Bichri; but the men of Judah joined with their king, from the Jordan even to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the men of Israel following Sheba while Judah stays with David. The quarrel has led to open revolt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the split as the bitter fruit of the dispute in the previous chapter. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober picture of division among God’s people.

verses.text: David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in custody and provided them with sustenance, but didn’t go in to them. So they were shut up to the day of their death, living in widowhood.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David placing the ten concubines in custody and providing for them, but having no further relations with them, so that they live in widowhood until death. The narrative records their lasting loss with restraint.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see their confinement as one of the costs of Absalom’s sin and the earlier prophecy against David’s house (2 Samuel 12:11). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sorrow for the women, without speculating beyond what the text says.
